title: In 1919 a wave of molasses swept through Boston and killed 21 people

cover.alt: A towering brown wave of molasses full of wreckage rolls down a Boston street under an elevated railway as a man in a fedora runs.

body: On 15 January 1919 a 50-foot steel tank in Boston's North End burst and released about 2.3 million gallons of molasses. A brown wave tore through the streets at about 35 mph, buckled the elevated railway and killed 21 people. The owner, United States Industrial Alcohol, blamed anarchists, but in 1925 a court-appointed auditor found the tank unsafe and the company liable. The official who oversaw its building had no engineering training, and the disaster helped bring in rules that engineers must sign off on such plans.

slides.alt: A street of brick warehouses under a steel elevated railway; behind it stands a huge riveted steel tank streaked with brown. People in caps, fedoras and a wide hat walk by.
slides.caption: Boston's North End, 15 January 1919: a mild 43°F. By Commercial Street stands a 50-foot steel tank holding 2.3 million gallons of molasses.

slides.alt: The steel tank splits open, its plates tearing apart and rivets flying, as a torrent of dark molasses bursts out.
slides.caption: About 12:30: “A dull, muffled roar gave but an instant's warning before the top of the tank was blown into the air.”

slides.alt: A towering brown wave full of broken planks sweeps down the street and buckles the elevated railway, as a man and a woman run in terror.
slides.caption: A wave of molasses, perhaps 15 to 25 feet high, sweeps through the streets at about 35 mph and smashes into the elevated railway.

slides.alt: The street is buried in thick molasses with wreckage everywhere. A policeman, a sailor and a workman wade waist-deep, reaching out to help.
slides.caption: The streets are buried 2 to 3 feet deep. “If a worker stood still for a minute he found himself glued to the ground.”

slides.alt: Firemen in dark coats hose the brown street with a powerful jet of water under the bent elevated railway.
slides.caption: 21 people die and about 150 are hurt. For weeks crews hose the streets with salt water from the harbour, which breaks the molasses down.

slides.alt: A courtroom with tall windows. Behind the bench sits the auditor; a witness points at a torn steel plate from the tank.
slides.caption: The company blames anarchists with a bomb. After years of hearings, the court's auditor rules in 1925: the tank was unsafe and the company is liable.

bubbles.text: It leaked from the start. Their fix? Paint it brown.
bubbles.speaker: A witness

slides.alt: An engineer points at a blueprint of a tank with dimension lines and a red stamp of approval.
slides.caption: The man in charge had no engineering training. The 50-foot tank was tested with 6 inches of water. Later rules made engineers sign off on such plans.

bubbles.text: From now on, a qualified engineer signs the plans. Novel idea.
bubbles.speaker: An engineer

slides.alt: A sunny park by the harbour with trees, and close up, a bronze plaque on a post.
slides.caption: Today the site is a park by the harbour, marked by a small plaque. No anarchist was ever found.

slides.question: What did the court-appointed auditor decide caused the flood?
slides.explanation: He rejected the company's bomb claim and found the tank unsafe: it was built without proper engineering, barely tested and leaked from the start.

source.label: City of Boston Archives: the molasses flood
